vignette: Rukmini had always been an active and engaged member of her community. As a non-profit worker at a local women's organization, she spent her days advocating for survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault. But despite her professional dedication to helping others heal from trauma, Rukmini had never spoken about her own experience with sexual assault, which occurred over 40 years ago when she was in college. As she navigated the quiet streets of her neighborhood on her daily walks, Rukmini couldn't shake off the feeling that she was being watched. She would often catch herself glancing over her shoulder, half-expecting to see someone lurking behind her. At night, she would lie awake, replaying memories of the assault in vivid detail - the sound of footsteps outside her dorm room door, the feel of rough hands on her skin, the smell of cheap cologne. Rukmini's husband, Raj, had grown increasingly concerned about her withdrawal from social activities and her growing reliance on sleep medication. He would try to engage her in conversations about their shared friends and family, but Rukmini found herself tuning out, lost in a sea of thoughts that seemed to swirl around the assault like a vortex. As a non-profit worker, Rukmini was no stranger to statistics on trauma recovery. She knew all about the importance of processing emotions and reframing negative self-talk. But as she sat at her desk each day, staring blankly at spreadsheets and grant proposals, Rukmini couldn't shake off the feeling that she was a hypocrite - advocating for others' healing while neglecting her own. Raj's gentle prodding had finally convinced Rukmini to seek help. As she sat in her therapist's office, surrounded by calming colors and soothing music, Rukmini felt a sense of trepidation wash over her. She was afraid that revisiting the past would unleash a torrent of emotions she wasn't prepared to handle. But as she began to speak about her experiences - hesitantly at first, then with growing urgency - Rukmini felt a weight slowly lifting off her shoulders. It was this fragile glimmer of hope that brought Rukmini to therapy, despite the fear of confronting the darkest corners of her own psyche. She knew it wouldn't be easy, but for the first time in decades, she felt willing to confront the assault head-on - not just as a distant memory, but as a lived experience that had shaped her into the person she was today.
